approachQuestion.prompt:
Shortest Delivery Segment

The array `deliveries` contains positive amounts from consecutive deliveries. Return the length of the shortest non-empty contiguous segment whose sum is at least `target`. Return 0 if no such segment exists. Keep the deliveries in their original order. Return only the length.

Limits and assumptions:
• 1 ≤ n ≤ 200000; 1 ≤ deliveries[i] ≤ 1000000; 1 ≤ target ≤ 10^12.
• Every value is strictly positive; sums fit in a 64-bit integer.
• The segment must be contiguous and non-empty.

Examples:
1. deliveries = [3,1,4,2,6], target = 8 → 2, for [2,6].
2. deliveries = [2,2,2], target = 7 → 0.

Choose one approach.
constraints: Every value is strictly positive; sums fit in a 64-bit integer.
The segment must be contiguous and non-empty.

options.text: Move the right boundary and add each delivery to the sum. Whenever the sum reaches the target, record the length and move the left boundary while the segment still meets the target.
options.feedback: Positive values make the sum non-decreasing when the segment grows and non-increasing when it shrinks from the left. These directions make both boundary moves safe.

options.text: Build increasing prefix sums, then use binary search for the first qualifying end for each start.
options.feedback: This works for every positive input and uses the increasing prefix sums, but it searches for the end separately for each start.

options.text: For each start, add the following deliveries until the sum reaches the target or the array ends; keep the shortest qualifying length.
options.feedback: The result is correct, but long segments are checked again for many different starts even though their boundaries can move together.

options.text: Sort deliveries from largest to smallest and choose the fewest largest values whose sum reaches the target.
options.feedback: Sorting loses the contiguity requirement. For [6,1,6] with target 12, the answer is 3; choosing the two largest deliveries does not form a contiguous segment.

feedback.reason: Check whether the window property and the boundary movements match the exact task conditions.

complexityQuestion.prompt: For the method “Move the right boundary and shrink the positive window,” choose one pair: running time and additional space.
constraints: Analyze only the named method. Do not count the input or returned value as additional space.
There is no recursion or call stack.

options.text: O(n log n) time, O(n) additional space

feedback.reason: Each value enters the window at most once and leaves it at most once. The method stores the boundaries, current sum, and best length.

details.correctness: Because every value is positive, extending the window cannot decrease its sum, and removing the leftmost value cannot increase it. Once the sum reaches the target, shrinking checks the shorter qualifying starts for that right boundary; discarded starts cannot later produce a better answer.
details.alternatives: Prefix sums with a separate search for each start are correct, but perform repeated searches. Enumerating starts and ends repeats work. Sorting breaks contiguity. The proof depends on strictly positive values: with arbitrary negative values, a boundary move can have the opposite effect. For example, [5,-10,8] contains the one-element segment [8] meeting target 7, even though the running prefix never reaches the target.

methodReveal.title: A positive window with moving boundaries
methodReveal.description: Add deliveries from the right and keep their sum. Whenever the sum reaches the target, record the length, then remove values from the left while the remaining segment still meets the target.
